name: E-Paper / E-Ink Surface
origin: The design is shaped by reflective, bistable displays: the panel can retain a static image without further power for image retention; the processor, radio and optional front light still consume energy. This entry depicts a deliberately monochrome reader variant. Grayscale, color range and refresh time depend on the panel and its driving mode: E Ink Kaleido, for example, combines 16 gray levels with 4096 colors, while TRMNL supports different device profiles. Software can composite transparency before output; this demo omits it as a design choice. Its warm paper colors and 16 named steps are a screen approximation, not a universal measurement of an e-paper panel.
idea: Contrast is not a design device but a capped resource: when ink never goes black and ground never goes white, and there is no color, no transparency and no motion, the whole hierarchy has to come out of size, weight, shape, fill level and inversion - and every halftone out of a dither grid instead of an alpha value.
markers: Demo ink #2B2B2B on paper #E4E2DD: about 10.9:1 rather than 21:1; not a universal e-paper ceiling
16 named steps in this demo; choose the actual count from the product device profile
No alpha anywhere: every halftone is an ordered dither (Bayer 4x4) on a 4px tile, no rgba, no opacity, no backdrop-filter
Demo stroke minimum 2px, with a 6px heading rule; check strokes on the target device because resolution and rendering vary
68px rows and page-by-page navigation in this demo; actual update time depends on panel, temperature and driving mode
Radius 0px without exception, 2px at most on buttons; no shadows, no layers, no blur - separation runs on 2px rules alone
Status never colored: filled 10px square for active, hollow for paused, half-dithered for blocked, always with the word spelled out beside it
Selection is the complete inversion of a row, hard and without transition - transition: none holds across the entire design
Pagination 'PAGE 1 / 4' instead of a scrollbar, because every refresh has to be paid for; paging is the only navigation metaphor

params.radius: 0px without exception, 2px at most on buttons
params.contrast: Demo palette: #2B2B2B on #E4E2DD gives about 10.9:1; physical panel contrast depends on the device and lighting
params.density: airy and latency-driven: 68px rows, 22px insets, pagination instead of scrolling
params.depth: none in this demo; 2px rules separate content on one plane, with alpha and shadows deliberately avoided
params.color: zero chroma: 16 gray levels with R=G=B (plus/minus 7 at the light end for the warm paper tone), no accent, no semantic color
params.type: proportional reading serif with a high x-height for content (Literata/Bookerly class), grotesque for chrome and labels; Regular and Semibold only, Light and Thin forbidden
params.motion: none - transition: none, no animation; state changes are hard switches, navigation is paging
params.texture: ordered dithering (Bayer 4x4) as the only halftone technique, 4px tile as data:image/svg+xml, levels 12.5 / 25 / 50 / 75%

examples.name: TRMNL Framework
examples.what: The hardest evidence, because it is a documented token language rather than a gut feeling: gray levels from --black #000000 through --gray-10 #111111 up to --gray-75 #EEEEEE and --white #FFFFFF, so 16 levels; gap scale 5/7/10/16/20/30/40px; default screen 800x480 at 1 bit; dedicated overrides for 2-bit, 4-bit and density 2x (Inter Variable there, on a 13px instead of a 16px base); elements Title/Value/Label/Description/Divider, components Table/Chart/Progress

examples.name: Amazon Kindle
examples.what: 16-level grayscale across every generation, on the Kindle 11 (2024) at 6 inches with 1072x1448 and 300 ppi; house serif Bookerly with a high x-height for long reading stretches; Colorsoft exposes the limit of color on these panels: 300 ppi in black and white against 150 ppi in color

examples.name: reMarkable
examples.what: Runs Codex, its own Linux-based operating system explicitly tuned for e-paper latency; reMarkable 2 at 10.3 inches and 1872x1404, Paper Pro at 11.8 inches and 2160x1620 with a Kaleido color layer; UI entirely without an accent tone, tool selection through filled against hollow symbols

examples.name: Light Phone II
examples.what: A 2.84-inch two-color E-Ink panel as the whole interface: the menu is a plain word list without icons, without badges, without color, selection through inversion; its successor, the Light Phone III, moved to AMOLED and left the language behind

examples.name: Electronic shelf labels
examples.what: The industrial, non-nostalgic mass case: price at maximum weight and size, unit price and unit two steps smaller, separation through thick solid rules instead of hairlines, state changes as a visible full refresh - hierarchy there comes exclusively out of size and position

strengths: The only entry with a contrast ceiling - it makes the catalog's parameter axis honest, where practically every other entry sits in the top third
Extremely cheap to build: two hex values, a 16-step ladder and a 4x4 Bayer tile; no color, no motion, no assets, no illustration
Robust to the point of insult: it works the same in sunlight, in grayscale print, on bad panels, on a fax, in a screenshot and in every contrast mode
Forces hierarchy through size, weight, shape, fill level and position - a discipline that carries over into every other language
Two quantities the catalog carries nowhere else are stated here in transferable terms: minimum stroke weight, and refresh cost as a layout dimension
Status is never communicated by color alone - simply because there is no color; that disposes of a whole class of accessibility bugs by itself
risks: Its representatives share no signature, only an absence. A Kindle, a reMarkable, an Onyx Boox, a shelf label and a TRMNL dashboard look precisely unlike one another in density, typographic character and layout logic - what unites them is 'no color, no motion, no shadow', and an entry defined only through deletions is blurry by construction

Worse: Kindle Colorsoft and reMarkable Paper Pro have color, A2 modes approach video rate, the Light Phone III moved to AMOLED - the hardware this style is derived from is currently abandoning its own premises
The contrast ceiling is a real accessibility risk: the middle steps of the ladder fall below 4.5:1 and are unusable for body text, even though the originals put them in exactly that place
On an ordinary emissive display the reflective effect that justifies the style is missing - the same design then reads quickly as a gray, half-charged or broken page
Without color there is no emergency signal: deletion, error and success look identical and have to be carried entirely by wording and placement
The 4px Bayer tile shimmers as soon as the browser scales the area by a non-integer factor - behind body text, dithering is therefore practically unusable
a11y: The darkest and lightest demo colors calculate to about 10.9:1; this does not measure the reflected contrast of a real panel. The metadata uses #5C5C5A instead of the overly light #757472. For a hardware implementation, check gray levels and dithering on the target device. The 2px strokes are a demo choice, not a WCAG minimum. Focus uses a 3px outline with a 4px offset; status uses both shape and wording. The demo has no motion. Disabled controls are exempt from contrast requirements, although their purpose should remain understandable.
longevity: Two parts with very different half-lives. The principle - capped contrast, hierarchy without color, halftone as a grid rather than an alpha value, minimum stroke weight - is at least as old as letterpress and 1-bit screens and will outlive every fashion cycle; as a design discipline it is timeless. The derivation from the hardware, by contrast, is already aging visibly: color E-Ink, faster refresh modes and the Light Phone's retreat from E-Ink are stripping the style of its justification step by step. Take it as a principle and you have something durable; take it as a device quotation and you have a window.

platforms.web: Very good - the whole language is two hex values, 2px borders and one SVG pattern; the only real adjustment is giving up every alpha utility, so no /10, no /20, no backdrop-blur, no shadow.
platforms.mobile: Mixed - the 68px rows and 52px controls are close to ideal for touch, but the style fights Material 3 head-on, with its dynamic color, ripple and elevation; on a bright OLED the capped contrast quickly reads as a rendering fault.
platforms.desktop: Good for a reading, writing or focus tool in Tauri, where calm is the point - bad for anything that needs status colors, charts or dense tables.

verdict: As the continuous language for a portfolio of small apps: no. Without status color, every error message, every destructive confirmation and every chart is a fight, and on a bright monitor you buy the capped contrast without the reflective advantage that justifies it. As a single, deliberately chosen mode, though, it is very strong and cheap to have: a reading view, a focus or night mode, a print and export view, or a dashboard that actually lands on a TRMNL or Inkplate panel - there it costs an afternoon and looks expensive immediately. The greatest value for a solo developer lies elsewhere, though: two weeks of building in this style is the best available exercise in producing hierarchy without color. What you learn there about size jumps, weight, fill level and white space carries every interface you build afterward - the colorful ones included. Concretely: as a mode yes, as a brand no, as an exercise absolutely.
tip: Build the ladder first and forbid alpha at the token level, not in review: sixteen named steps from ink to ground, and not a single color function with a fourth component in the whole project. Then implement the halftone exactly once as a parameterized 4x4 Bayer tile and derive every area shading from it. The mistake almost everyone makes is stroke weight: icon sets ship with 1.5px or 1px strokes, and those are the lines that make a design fray. Redraw every icon at 2px or take a different set - that is more work than the entire palette, and it makes the difference between 'like E-Ink' and 'like a grayscale theme turned up too bright'.

finder.signature: Selection inverts the whole row; you page instead of scrolling, because every refresh costs time.
